thread.title: As earnings arrive, tech CEOs have a lot of explaining to do

author: Therese Poletti
title: As earnings arrive, tech CEOs have a lot of explaining to do
text:
Tech’s annual victory parade is likely to turn into an apology tour in the next few weeks, as executives in charge of some of the most important companies in America face investors with much more to discuss than record-breaking holiday-shopping results. 
Tech executives have already been performing public apologies in response to two huge controversies: The potential impact from major flaws in semiconductor design disclosed earlier this month, and how social networks are combating counterfeit news. Now, they will have to explain exactly how these flaws and their proposed fixes will affect their earnings to anxious investors and an angry public.
The question for investors is which will matter more: The huge revenue and profit from fourth-quarter results, or the long-term fallout from Big Tech’s missteps.
Haunted by Spectre 
Semiconductor giant Intel Corp. INTC, +1.46% INTC, +1.46% will be the one of the first tech giants to report results on Jan, 25, just weeks after two major flaws in microprocessor designs were reported by three separate groups of researchers . A design trick used to speed up the processor is now seen as having a flaw that can leave core memory in PCs and servers exposed, and make them vulnerable to hackers. Fixes can slow down systems, in rare cases causing as much as a 30% drop in performance. 
Intel has been developing firmware patches for its microprocessors, which are the most impacted by the flaws. Only Intel chips appear to be impacted by the vulnerability dubbed Meltdown, while a second vulnerability, called Spectre, affects both Intel chips and chips from other companies like Advanced Micro Devices Inc. AMD, +0.56% and ARM Holdings, now owned by SoftBank Group Corp. 9984, +0.95% 
Don’t miss: Which devices are at risk from Meltdown and Spectre, and what can you do to safeguard them? 
“It remains early days, and we will undoubtedly hear more over time as more work is done, fixes are optimized, etc.; we also await further similar analysis on competitors’ solutions,” Stacy Rasgon, a Bernstein Research analyst, said in a recent note. “At a minimum, we appreciate that Intel is attempting to be transparent on the issue given the potentially wide-ranging implications it could conceivably have on the industry.”
It is unlikely that investors will get any sense of the financial implications of the flaw at this early stage, but the biggest fear for Intel investors is that its biggest customers, such as cloud-computing service providers and its other data center customers, will begin to look elsewhere for new chips to upgrade their data centers. And AMD may benefit from any decisions to diversify the technology in the data center, just having launched a new server chip.
Read also: At CES, Spectre haunted tech executives in public and private 
Investors and analysts are hoping to get some idea on how tech’s corporate customers are reacting to the issues. Any commentary or response from Intel, AMD, which reports on Jan. 30, and Microsoft Corp. MSFT, +1.17% which had to develop software patches as well, will be of key importance. The first public statement from Intel Chief Executive Brian Krzanich on his fishy stock sales would certainly be appreciated. 
Microsoft, which reports Jan. 31, is in the unique position of being both a vendor of PC and server software that it is having to fix and a customer for its own data centers for cloud-computing services, so it may be in the best position to give some frank input on the issue. 
Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, +1.63% will also likely be asked about any impacts to performance at its Amazon Web Services business and how customers are reacting. The e-commerce company is typically reticent to say anything of import during earnings reports and conference calls, however, so it is unlikely it will disclose much about the impact.
The online controversies 
The other big issue hanging over tech balance sheets are changes that Facebook Inc. FB, +1.64% Alphabet Inc.’s GOOG, +1.90% GOOGL, +1.97% YouTube and Twitter Inc. TWTR, -1.31% are deploying to combat counterfeit news in their networks. Facebook said it was completely revamping its newsfeed, likely the biggest change to the social network since its IPO in 2012 , to prioritize posts from family and friends, at the expense of news, in an effort to combat the dissemination of fabricated information. Analysts are clearly worried about the impact the move will have on advertising revenue, and Facebook’s Jan. 31 earnings report will give the company a chance to address the financial implications of its big move with depth. 
Don’t miss: How Facebook’s News Feed change is stoking uncertainty about its future 
Alphabet executives will likely discuss the YouTube business impact from its decision on Tuesday to beef up human oversight of its content and reduce the number of channels that may show ads wen it reports Feb. 1. So far, though, investors are not expecting a big impact to its overall revenue, which is not yet broken out by Alphabet, based on how the company fared last year when it was hit with some boycotting by advertisers over inappropriate content. 
Late Friday, Twitter added to the fray of dealing with counterfeit news, saying in a blog post that even more accounts than identified previously were associated with spreading misinformation during the U.S. presidential election. Beyond the news on its platform, Twitter is already under the microscope after admitting that the metrics it has provided investors for years were not accurate . That company will report a week after Facebook and Alphabet, on Feb. 8.
The numbers may be all that matters 
The biggest tech company of them all, Apple Inc., AAPL, -0.62% has had its own issues in the past few months, including admitting that a software update slowed down iPhones with degraded batteries . CEO Tim Cook managed to change the discussion around his company with news that Apple will pay $38 billion in taxes on its repatriated funds, getting ahead of the flood of tax-related discussions that will also be repeatedly addressed in earnings reports.
Read: Apple didn’t say it was hiring 20,000 new workers, nor bringing back all of its overseas cash 
Despite the controversy over slowed-down iPhones and all of Apple’s promises to invest in the U.S., the focus for Apple investors seems to be more on iPhone sales, which are supposed to lead to record sales after the launch of the $1,000 iPhone X. Other companies can only hope that investors also focus on their impressive earnings instead of tech’s hot-button issues of the moment.
